NYSCA and NYFA Launch 2026 Cycle of NYSCA Reserve Fund Grants  
First -of-its-kind program was established by NYSCA in 2025 to support NYS arts and culture nonprofits 
and address critical needs across the state’s creative sector. 
 
The New York State Council on the Arts  (NYSCA) and the New York Foundation for the Arts  (NYFA) today 
announced the 2026 cycle of NYSCA Reserve Fund Grants  (RFG), an innovative initiative designed to help 
New York State-based nonprofit arts organizations to establish a reserve fund or build on an existing reserve 
fund.  
Grants of up to $50,000 will be made available for a total of $1,760,000 in support. Organizations that have 
received funding from NYSCA in the last three years (FY24-FY26) with operating budgets of $150K to $3M will 
be eligible to apply.  
Organizational reserves are foundational to the economic strength of New York’s arts and culture sector. 
Through strategic funding opportunities like the RFG, organizations address the challenges and concerns facing the arts and culture sector head-on, like increased costs, decreased philanthropy, and unpredictable 
income. Reserve funds  sustain public access  to arts and culture, cover the unexpected, strengthen balance 
sheets to leverage new funders, and make space for organizations and artists to do what they do best - c reate.   
Applications will open on Tuesday, March 10 at 10:00 AM ET and close on Tuesday, May 5 at 5:00 PM ET and will be available through the NYFA website. 
Organizations that choose to use grant funds to start a reserve fund and do not already have one at the time of 
applying are prioritized. R ural and BIPOC -led community -based organizations are strongly encouraged to 
apply. Grant amounts will be determined by the organization’s overall operating budget. Organizations that are 
fiscally sponsored by another 501(c)(3) are ineligible for this opportunity. 
NYSCA Executive Director Erika Mallin said,  “The success of the first year of this program was  clear – over 
1200 applicants and 85% of grantees building their very first cash reserve, a powerful affirmation to how 
urgently these funds are needed. Organizations with strong reserves are organizations empowered to 
innovate, to plan, and to deliver the measurable benefits of the arts to their communities. We are proud to 
partner with NYFA on this critical program for a second year, providing nonprofits with the continuity and long-
term sustainability they need to thrive.” 
 

  
 
 
411 Fifth Avenue, New York, NY 10016  | arts.ny.gov    NYSCA Chair Patrick Willingham said, “The NYSCA Reserve Fund is a rare and powerful opportunity for 
arts and culture nonprofits to build the financial foundation they need to keep their doors open, their programs 
running and their audience growing. I encourage every eligible organization to apply and help us ensure our 
arts and culture sector remains vibrant and resilient for generations to come.” 
Michael Royce, NYFA CEO, said “We are grateful to Governor Hochul for continuing to invest in and 
strengthen the arts across New York State, and to NYSCA for partnering with us on this groundbreaking 
program. Reserve Fund Grants are helping to build a more sustainable future for arts organizations and the 
many communities they serve,” he added. 
In addition to providing support through direct funds, the RFG will offer one year of tec hnical  assistance  
focused on organizational sustainability and financial prudence. Each recipient will receive:  
● One virtual workshop dedicated to organizational reserve funding and strategies to support long- term 
sustainability . 
● One hour long one-on-one consulting session. 
● Monthly office hours to field pressing questions in a communal setting. 
 
Eligible applications undergo a three-round review and elimination process. All applicants will be notified, 
regardless of the outcome, by Fall 2026. 
On receiving the award in 2025, Stockade Works  (Kingston) Founder Mary Stuart Masterson said: “Reserve 
funds are incredibly challenging to build, and opportunities like the NYSCA Reserve Fund Grant are nearly 
nonexistent, making this a rare chance for our organization to take a step forward. The grant has also been a 
motivating factor in establishing a Reserve Fund Policy, which coupled with the seed funding, will enable 
Stockade Works to thoughtfully build real financial stability, plan for the future, and remain strong for our 
community during a time when all nonprofits are facing instability and uncertainty.”  
For 2025 recipient Art Beyond Sight, the grant will help to ensure that disability -led innovation remains a vital 
part of New York’s cultural landscape. Said Founder Elisabeth Axel: “For a small nonprofit leading large-scale accessibility efforts, this safety net is more than financial —it is a foundation for resilience, allowing us to 
deepen our learnings as to how to plan responsibly for the future. Equally significant is the advice and guidance that accompany this grant.”  
For those interested in applying, the NYFA Grants team will host virtual information sessions designed to help 
organizations  understand if they are eligible and how to build a strong application.  
The first session will take place on Thursday, March 19 at 2:00 PM ET and will dive deeper into the importance 
of building reserve funds. The second session is scheduled for Tuesday, March 31 at 2:00 PM ET and focus 
on a general application and guidelines overview. All info sessions are held virtually over Zoom, are free to 
attend, and are presented in English. Registration is required.

About New York Foundation for the Arts (NYFA):  
The New York Foundation for the Arts (NYFA) was established in 1971 to empower artists at critical stages in 
their creative lives. Today, the nonprofit organization’s programs and services are far-reaching and are rooted 
in a wealth of physical and online resources. Each year, NYFA awards more than $4 million in cash grants to 

  
 
 
411 Fifth Avenue, New York, NY 10016  | arts.ny.gov    individual visual, performing, and literary artists throughout the United States. NYFA’s Fiscal Sponsorship 
program, one of the oldest and most reputable in the country, helps national artists and arts organizations raise 
and manage an average of $4 million annually. NYFA’s Learning programs, including its Artist as Entrepreneur 
and Immigrant Artist Mentoring Program, provide thousands of artists, creatives, and arts administrators with 
professional development training and support. NYFA’s website, NYFA.org , is used by more than 1 million 
people and features more than 20,000 opportunities and resources available to artists in all disciplines.  
About the New York State Council on the Arts 
The mission of the New York State Council on the Arts is to foster and advance the full breadth of New York 
State’s arts, culture and creativity for all. For FY 2026, the Council on the Arts will award over $161 million, 
serving organizations and artists across all 10 of the state’s regions. The Council on the Arts further advances 
New York’s creative culture by convening leaders in the field and providing organizational and professional 
development opportunities and informational resources. Created by Governor Nelson Rockefeller in 1960 and 
continued with the support of Governor Hochul and the New York State Legislature, the Council is an agency 
that is part of the Executive Branch. For more information on NYSCA, please visit arts.ny.gov/SOAfellow , and 
follow NYSCA’s Facebook page, on X @NYSCArts  and Instagram @NYSCouncilontheArts .

Meet the First State of the Arts Fellows: The New York State Council on the Arts Announces the Three 
Artists to Collaborate with State Agencies  
Governor’s Initiative Places Artists to Work Alongside State Agencies for Creative Problem Solving  
The New York State Council on the Arts has announced the three inaugural fellows for the State of the Arts 
Fellowship Program. A new initiative from Governor Kathy Hochul, the State of the Arts Fellowship Program 
embeds NYS artists into state agencies to collaborate and develop creative solutions to specific agency 
challenges.  
The inaugural placements are:  
• Polymedia artist Eto Otitigbe (Brooklyn) will work alongside the Office of General Services (OGS)  to 
revitalize Empire State Plaza in Albany with creative, community focused programming.  
 
• Cara Hanley  (Albany), a community -based artist and licensed social worker, will partner with the Office 
of Mental Health (OMH) to destigmatize mental health issues and promote access to OMH services.  
 
• Interdisciplinary artist sTo Len (Glendale) and the Office of Victim Services (OVS)  will increase 
awareness among underserved populations of the Fair Access to Victim Compensation Act.  
Through a collaborative process, the fellows will work closely with State agencies to create new avenues for communication and connection, while highlighting the potential for innovative, cross -disciplinary solutions that 
leave a lasting impact on communities across New York. The program received over 400 applications from 
across the state. These inaugural projects are expected to be completed by March 2027. The next State of the 
Arts Fellowship opportunity will be announced by Summer 2026. Details will be posted at arts.ny.gov .  
For more information about each artist, please visit https://arts.ny.gov/SOAfellow . 
NYSCA Executive Director Erika Mallin said, “As critical thinkers and thought leaders, artists bring unique perspectives that help us reimagine solutions to our most pressing social challenges. NYSCA is proud to bring 
this important Governor’s initiative to our fellow agencies and look forward to the groundbreaking work that will 
emerge from these collaborations.”  
NYSCA Chair Patrick Willingham said, “This program is a powerful statement about the value of the artist  in 
New York State.  Not just an opportunity  for collaboration,  the Fellowship program  recognizes 
the critical importance of  creative  practice to better our everyday lives. Congratulations to all the inaugural 
fellows.”   

  
 
 
411 Fifth Avenue, New York, NY 10016  | arts.ny.gov    Office of General Services Commissioner Jeanette Moy said, "OGS is dedicated to strengthening the 
Empire State Plaza's ties with its surrounding communities and enhancing our public spaces to be more 
inclusive, dynamic, and representative of New York's diversity. We look forward to partnering with fellow Eto 
Otitigbe, an artist with roots in Albany. H is artistic practice thoughtfully blends history, community, and the 
natural world, key components of our Reconnect the Plaza initiative. We are grateful to Governor Hochul and NYSCA for this invaluable opportunity to introduce fresh perspectives to this space and foster further 
engagement with our neighbors.”  
 
Office of Mental Health Commissioner Dr. Ann Sullivan said,  “There is such a healing component to art. It 
is especially impactful in supporting Individuals on their path to recovery from mental health concerns. Art also 
is a universal language with the transformative power to change perceptions about mental illness and 
recovery. We are delighted to be one of three host agencies for the New York State of the Arts Fellowship, 
enabling us to combine these two benefits to support recovery and reduce stigma. Fellow Cara Hanley has 
been specifically chosen for her experience in the mental health field and her artistic talent that will further our 
vision of increased appreciation, understanding and empathy of mental health and recovery. By engaging 
individuals in recovery alongside mental health care providers, this work will promote healing, affirm individual 
strengths, support self -determination and increase the understanding of mental health as a foundation for 
inclusive and resilient communities. This inspiring project demonstrates how Governor Hochul is highlighting 
the important work of state agencies through the creative arts.”   
Office of Victim Services Director Bea Hanson said,  “OVS is proud to welcome sTo Len as our selected 
artist for this statewide fellowship program. His multidisciplinary, community -centered approach aligns with our 
mission to ensure survivors of crime and their families can access the services and support they need. We look 
forward to partnering with him to explore new, creative ways to increase awareness, reduce barriers, and 
strengthen connections between OVS and communities across New York.”   
NY State of the Arts Fellow Eto Otitigbe said , “I grew up in Albany, and the art and architecture of the 
Empire State Plaza shaped my imagination and inspired my creative journey. Over the years  I’ve shared my 
work internationally, and this fellowship offers the opportunity to bring those experiences back to my roots. The 
Plaza and the surrounding communities hold layered civic and historical narratives that deserve deeper 
attention. I want to activate the site’s sensory and spatial qualities to tell those stories in collaboration with local 
creatives and the OGS.  
NY State of the Arts Fellow Cara Hanley said,  "Art has the unique ability to make the invisible visible. It can 
transform how we understand mental health: not as a deficit, but as a space for growth, resilience, and individuality. Through this fellowship, I aim to create work that not only uplifts the voices of those within the OMH system but also encourages broader community empathy, reduces stigma, and helps more people feel 
safe accessing support. This opportunity represents the heart of what I strive for: honoring the full humanity of 
those living with mental health challenges through creative practice."
 
NY State of the Arts Fellow sTo Len said,  "As an artist, I am deeply committed to unconventional civic 
investigations that can help build a more creative relationship between our government and everyday citizens. 
The vast  assistance that the Office of Victim Services provides survivors of  crime  and their families are 
essential services of care that must be accessible to all who may need it.  I’m excited to work on creating new 
ways of connecting survivors of crime to OVS through art that acknowledges their resilience and advocates for their rights. How might we reimagine a state agency as an ally and a safe space to those in need and break

First -of-its-kind program was established by NYSCA in 2025 to support NYS arts and culture nonprofits 
and address critical needs across the state’s creative sector. 
 
The New York State Council on the Arts  (NYSCA) and the New York Foundation for the Arts  (NYFA) today 
announced the 2026 cycle of NYSCA Reserve Fund Grants  (RFG), an innovative initiative designed to help 
New York State-based nonprofit arts organizations to establish a reserve fund or build on an existing reserve 
fund.  
Grants of up to $50,000 will be made available for a total of $1,760,000 in support. Organizations that have 
received funding from NYSCA in the last three years (FY24-FY26) with operating budgets of $150K to $3M will 
be eligible to apply.  
Organizational reserves are foundational to the economic strength of New York’s arts and culture sector. 
Through strategic funding opportunities like the RFG, organizations address the challenges and concerns facing the arts and culture sector head-on, like increased costs, decreased philanthropy, and unpredictable 
income. Reserve funds  sustain public access  to arts and culture, cover the unexpected, strengthen balance 
sheets to leverage new funders, and make space for organizations and artists to do what they do best - c reate.   
Applications will open on Tuesday, March 10 at 10:00 AM ET and close on Tuesday, May 5 at 5:00 PM ET and will be available through the NYFA website. 
Organizations that choose to use grant funds to start a reserve fund and do not already have one at the time of 
applying are prioritized. R ural and BIPOC -led community -based organizations are strongly encouraged to 
apply. Grant amounts will be determined by the organization’s overall operating budget. Organizations that are 
fiscally sponsored by another 501(c)(3) are ineligible for this opportunity. 
NYSCA Executive Director Erika Mallin said,  “The success of the first year of this program was  clear – over 
1200 applicants and 85% of grantees building their very first cash reserve, a powerful affirmation to how 
urgently these funds are needed. Organizations with strong reserves are organizations empowered to 
innovate, to plan, and to deliver the measurable benefits of the arts to their communities. We are proud to 
partner with NYFA on this critical program for a second year, providing nonprofits with the continuity and long-
term sustainability they need to thrive.” 
 

  
 
 
411 Fifth Avenue, New York, NY 10016  | arts.ny.gov    NYSCA Chair Patrick Willingham said, “The NYSCA Reserve Fund is a rare and powerful opportunity for 
arts and culture nonprofits to build the financial foundation they need to keep their doors open, their programs 
running and their audience growing. I encourage every eligible organization to apply and help us ensure our 
arts and culture sector remains vibrant and resilient for generations to come.” 
Michael Royce, NYFA CEO, said “We are grateful to Governor Hochul for continuing to invest in and 
strengthen the arts across New York State, and to NYSCA for partnering with us on this groundbreaking 
program. Reserve Fund Grants are helping to build a more sustainable future for arts organizations and the 
many communities they serve,” he added. 
In addition to providing support through direct funds, the RFG will offer one year of tec hnical  assistance  
focused on organizational sustainability and financial prudence. Each recipient will receive:  
● One virtual workshop dedicated to organizational reserve funding and strategies to support long- term 
sustainability . 
● One hour long one-on-one consulting session. 
● Monthly office hours to field pressing questions in a communal setting. 
 
Eligible applications undergo a three-round review and elimination process. All applicants will be notified, 
regardless of the outcome, by Fall 2026. 
On receiving the award in 2025, Stockade Works  (Kingston) Founder Mary Stuart Masterson said: “Reserve 
funds are incredibly challenging to build, and opportunities like the NYSCA Reserve Fund Grant are nearly 
nonexistent, making this a rare chance for our organization to take a step forward. The grant has also been a 
motivating factor in establishing a Reserve Fund Policy, which coupled with the seed funding, will enable 
Stockade Works to thoughtfully build real financial stability, plan for the future, and remain strong for our 
community during a time when all nonprofits are facing instability and uncertainty.”

part of New York’s cultural landscape. Said Founder Elisabeth Axel: “For a small nonprofit leading large-scale accessibility efforts, this safety net is more than financial —it is a foundation for resilience, allowing us to 
deepen our learnings as to how to plan responsibly for the future. Equally significant is the advice and guidance that accompany this grant.”

of building reserve funds. The second session is scheduled for Tuesday, March 31 at 2:00 PM ET and focus 
on a general application and guidelines overview. All info sessions are held virtually over Zoom, are free to 
attend, and are presented in English. Registration is required.

grants.description: The NYSCA Reserve Fund Grants (RFG) program is designed to help New York State-based nonprofit arts organizations establish or enhance reserve funds. Grants of up to $50,000 are available, with a total funding pool of $1,760,000. Priority is given to organizations starting reserve funds for the first time, as well as rural and BIPOC-led community-based organizations. Eligible organizations must have received NYSCA funding in the last three years and have operating budgets between $150,000 and $3 million. Applications are reviewed in three rounds, and all applicants will be notified of the outcome by Fall 2026. Technical assistance, including workshops and consulting, is provided to recipients.

NYSCA and NYFA Launch 2026 Cycle of NYSCA Reserve Fund Grants  
First -of-its-kind program was established by NYSCA in 2025 to support NYS arts and culture nonprofits 
and address critical needs across the state’s creative sector. 
 
The New York State Council on the Arts  (NYSCA) and the New York Foundation for the Arts  (NYFA) today 
announced the 2026 cycle of NYSCA Reserve Fund Grants  (RFG), an innovative initiative designed to help 
New York State-based nonprofit arts organizations to establish a reserve fund or build on an existing reserve 
fund.  
Grants of up to $50,000 will be made available for a total of $1,760,000 in support. Organizations that have 
received funding from NYSCA in the last three years (FY24-FY26) with operating budgets of $150K to $3M will 
be eligible to apply.  
Organizational reserves are foundational to the economic strength of New York’s arts and culture sector. 
Through strategic funding opportunities like the RFG, organizations address the challenges and concerns facing the arts and culture sector head-on, like increased costs, decreased philanthropy, and unpredictable 
income. Reserve funds  sustain public access  to arts and culture, cover the unexpected, strengthen balance 
sheets to leverage new funders, and make space for organizations and artists to do what they do best - c reate.   
Applications will open on Tuesday, March 10 at 10:00 AM ET and close on Tuesday, May 5 at 5:00 PM ET and will be available through the NYFA website. 
Organizations that choose to use grant funds to start a reserve fund and do not already have one at the time of 
applying are prioritized. R ural and BIPOC -led community -based organizations are strongly encouraged to 
apply. Grant amounts will be determined by the organization’s overall operating budget. Organizations that are 
fiscally sponsored by another 501(c)(3) are ineligible for this opportunity. 
NYSCA Executive Director Erika Mallin said,  “The success of the first year of this program was  clear – over 
1200 applicants and 85% of grantees building their very first cash reserve, a powerful affirmation to how 
urgently these funds are needed. Organizations with strong reserves are organizations empowered to 
innovate, to plan, and to deliver the measurable benefits of the arts to their communities. We are proud to 
partner with NYFA on this critical program for a second year, providing nonprofits with the continuity and long-
term sustainability they need to thrive.” 
 

  
 
 
411 Fifth Avenue, New York, NY 10016  | arts.ny.gov    NYSCA Chair Patrick Willingham said, “The NYSCA Reserve Fund is a rare and powerful opportunity for 
arts and culture nonprofits to build the financial foundation they need to keep their doors open, their programs 
running and their audience growing. I encourage every eligible organization to apply and help us ensure our 
arts and culture sector remains vibrant and resilient for generations to come.” 
Michael Royce, NYFA CEO, said “We are grateful to Governor Hochul for continuing to invest in and 
strengthen the arts across New York State, and to NYSCA for partnering with us on this groundbreaking 
program. Reserve Fund Grants are helping to build a more sustainable future for arts organizations and the 
many communities they serve,” he added. 
In addition to providing support through direct funds, the RFG will offer one year of tec hnical  assistance  
focused on organizational sustainability and financial prudence. Each recipient will receive:  
● One virtual workshop dedicated to organizational reserve funding and strategies to support long- term 
sustainability . 
● One hour long one-on-one consulting session. 
● Monthly office hours to field pressing questions in a communal setting. 
 
Eligible applications undergo a three-round review and elimination process. All applicants will be notified, 
regardless of the outcome, by Fall 2026. 
On receiving the award in 2025, Stockade Works  (Kingston) Founder Mary Stuart Masterson said: “Reserve 
funds are incredibly challenging to build, and opportunities like the NYSCA Reserve Fund Grant are nearly 
nonexistent, making this a rare chance for our organization to take a step forward. The grant has also been a 
motivating factor in establishing a Reserve Fund Policy, which coupled with the seed funding, will enable 
Stockade Works to thoughtfully build real financial stability, plan for the future, and remain strong for our 
community during a time when all nonprofits are facing instability and uncertainty.”  
For 2025 recipient Art Beyond Sight, the grant will help to ensure that disability -led innovation remains a vital 
part of New York’s cultural landscape. Said Founder Elisabeth Axel: “For a small nonprofit leading large-scale accessibility efforts, this safety net is more than financial —it is a foundation for resilience, allowing us to 
deepen our learnings as to how to plan responsibly for the future. Equally significant is the advice and guidance that accompany this grant.”  
For those interested in applying, the NYFA Grants team will host virtual information sessions designed to help 
organizations  understand if they are eligible and how to build a strong application.  
The first session will take place on Thursday, March 19 at 2:00 PM ET and will dive deeper into the importance 
of building reserve funds. The second session is scheduled for Tuesday, March 31 at 2:00 PM ET and focus 
on a general application and guidelines overview. All info sessions are held virtually over Zoom, are free to 
attend, and are presented in English. Registration is required.

The New York Foundation for the Arts (NYFA) was established in 1971 to empower artists at critical stages in 
their creative lives. Today, the nonprofit organization’s programs and services are far-reaching and are rooted 
in a wealth of physical and online resources. Each year, NYFA awards more than $4 million in cash grants to

and Immigrant Artist Mentoring Program, provide thousands of artists, creatives, and arts administrators with 
professional development training and support. NYFA’s website, NYFA.org , is used by more than 1 million 
people and features more than 20,000 opportunities and resources available to artists in all disciplines.

Meet the First State of the Arts Fellows: The New York State Council on the Arts Announces the Three 
Artists to Collaborate with State Agencies  
Governor’s Initiative Places Artists to Work Alongside State Agencies for Creative Problem Solving  
The New York State Council on the Arts has announced the three inaugural fellows for the State of the Arts 
Fellowship Program. A new initiative from Governor Kathy Hochul, the State of the Arts Fellowship Program 
embeds NYS artists into state agencies to collaborate and develop creative solutions to specific agency 
challenges.  
The inaugural placements are:  
• Polymedia artist Eto Otitigbe (Brooklyn) will work alongside the Office of General Services (OGS)  to 
revitalize Empire State Plaza in Albany with creative, community focused programming.  
 
• Cara Hanley  (Albany), a community -based artist and licensed social worker, will partner with the Office 
of Mental Health (OMH) to destigmatize mental health issues and promote access to OMH services.  
 
• Interdisciplinary artist sTo Len (Glendale) and the Office of Victim Services (OVS)  will increase 
awareness among underserved populations of the Fair Access to Victim Compensation Act.  
Through a collaborative process, the fellows will work closely with State agencies to create new avenues for communication and connection, while highlighting the potential for innovative, cross -disciplinary solutions that 
leave a lasting impact on communities across New York. The program received over 400 applications from 
across the state. These inaugural projects are expected to be completed by March 2027. The next State of the 
Arts Fellowship opportunity will be announced by Summer 2026. Details will be posted at arts.ny.gov .  
For more information about each artist, please visit https://arts.ny.gov/SOAfellow . 
NYSCA Executive Director Erika Mallin said, “As critical thinkers and thought leaders, artists bring unique perspectives that help us reimagine solutions to our most pressing social challenges. NYSCA is proud to bring 
this important Governor’s initiative to our fellow agencies and look forward to the groundbreaking work that will 
emerge from these collaborations.”  
NYSCA Chair Patrick Willingham said, “This program is a powerful statement about the value of the artist  in 
New York State.  Not just an opportunity  for collaboration,  the Fellowship program  recognizes 
the critical importance of  creative  practice to better our everyday lives. Congratulations to all the inaugural 
fellows.”   

  
 
 
411 Fifth Avenue, New York, NY 10016  | arts.ny.gov    Office of General Services Commissioner Jeanette Moy said, "OGS is dedicated to strengthening the 
Empire State Plaza's ties with its surrounding communities and enhancing our public spaces to be more 
inclusive, dynamic, and representative of New York's diversity. We look forward to partnering with fellow Eto 
Otitigbe, an artist with roots in Albany. H is artistic practice thoughtfully blends history, community, and the 
natural world, key components of our Reconnect the Plaza initiative. We are grateful to Governor Hochul and NYSCA for this invaluable opportunity to introduce fresh perspectives to this space and foster further 
engagement with our neighbors.”  
 
Office of Mental Health Commissioner Dr. Ann Sullivan said,  “There is such a healing component to art. It 
is especially impactful in supporting Individuals on their path to recovery from mental health concerns. Art also 
is a universal language with the transformative power to change perceptions about mental illness and 
recovery. We are delighted to be one of three host agencies for the New York State of the Arts Fellowship, 
enabling us to combine these two benefits to support recovery and reduce stigma. Fellow Cara Hanley has 
been specifically chosen for her experience in the mental health field and her artistic talent that will further our 
vision of increased appreciation, understanding and empathy of mental health and recovery. By engaging 
individuals in recovery alongside mental health care providers, this work will promote healing, affirm individual 
strengths, support self -determination and increase the understanding of mental health as a foundation for 
inclusive and resilient communities. This inspiring project demonstrates how Governor Hochul is highlighting 
the important work of state agencies through the creative arts.”   
Office of Victim Services Director Bea Hanson said,  “OVS is proud to welcome sTo Len as our selected 
artist for this statewide fellowship program. His multidisciplinary, community -centered approach aligns with our 
mission to ensure survivors of crime and their families can access the services and support they need. We look 
forward to partnering with him to explore new, creative ways to increase awareness, reduce barriers, and 
strengthen connections between OVS and communities across New York.”   
NY State of the Arts Fellow Eto Otitigbe said , “I grew up in Albany, and the art and architecture of the 
Empire State Plaza shaped my imagination and inspired my creative journey. Over the years  I’ve shared my 
work internationally, and this fellowship offers the opportunity to bring those experiences back to my roots. The 
Plaza and the surrounding communities hold layered civic and historical narratives that deserve deeper 
attention. I want to activate the site’s sensory and spatial qualities to tell those stories in collaboration with local 
creatives and the OGS.  
NY State of the Arts Fellow Cara Hanley said,  "Art has the unique ability to make the invisible visible. It can 
transform how we understand mental health: not as a deficit, but as a space for growth, resilience, and individuality. Through this fellowship, I aim to create work that not only uplifts the voices of those within the OMH system but also encourages broader community empathy, reduces stigma, and helps more people feel 
safe accessing support. This opportunity represents the heart of what I strive for: honoring the full humanity of 
those living with mental health challenges through creative practice."
 
NY State of the Arts Fellow sTo Len said,  "As an artist, I am deeply committed to unconventional civic 
investigations that can help build a more creative relationship between our government and everyday citizens. 
The vast  assistance that the Office of Victim Services provides survivors of  crime  and their families are 
essential services of care that must be accessible to all who may need it.  I’m excited to work on creating new 
ways of connecting survivors of crime to OVS through art that acknowledges their resilience and advocates for their rights. How might we reimagine a state agency as an ally and a safe space to those in need and break
